data.rationale: The agreement specified five SEO articles and a four‑email sequence for $1,500. Articles 1‑4 and the email sequence were uploaded on schedule, approved by the client, and published on the client’s site, proving that the majority of the service was delivered as described and was used. The only missing deliverable is Article 5, which was never uploaded and the freelancer stopped responding after Sep 8, creating the client’s impression of abandonment. Therefore the client is entitled only to a proportional refund for the undelivered article ($250), and the rest of the chargeback should be contested.

proof_plan.point: The contract explicitly described the deliverables as five SEO blog articles (1,200‑1,500 words each) and a four‑email welcome sequence.
All four of the first articles and the email sequence were uploaded on the agreed dates and approved by the buyer, showing compliance with the described service.
The buyer explicitly approved each delivered piece (Articles 1‑4 and the email sequence) via email confirmations dated Aug‑13, Aug‑19, Aug‑29, Sep‑1, and Sep‑3.
The delivered articles have been published on the client’s website and the email sequence is live, demonstrating that the work was used and fit for purpose.
Article 5 was never uploaded; the delivery log shows no file for Article 5 as of 2026‑10‑10, constituting the undelivered portion of the contract.

After informing the client on Sep 8 that he was ill and would deliver Article 5 by Sep 12, the freelancer failed to respond to the client’s follow‑up messages on Sep 16 and Sep 24, creating the impression of abandonment.

data.resolution_action: Deliver the missing Article 5 to the client within 5 business days; if the client declines the delivery, issue a $250.00 refund.

evidences.notes:
The agreement between Jordan Kim and Nadia Rossi clearly defined the deliverables as five SEO blog articles of 1,200‑1,500 words each and a four‑email welcome sequence. [1]

The disputed PayPal transaction of $1,500.00 USD (invoice JKC-088) was paid on 2026‑08‑05 in full accordance with the contract price of $250 per article plus $250 for the email sequence. [2][3]

Article 1 was uploaded on 2026‑08‑12 and approved by the buyer on Aug 13; Article 2 was uploaded on 2026‑08‑19 and approved the same day; Article 3 was uploaded on 2026‑08‑26, revised, and approved on Aug 29; Article 4 was uploaded on 2026‑09‑02 and approved on Sep 3; the 4‑email sequence was uploaded on 2026‑08‑30 and approved on Sep 1. [4][5][6][7][8]

All four delivered articles have been published on the client’s blog and the email sequence is live, confirming that the work was used and fit for its intended purpose. [9][10]

Article 5 was never uploaded; the delivery log shows no file for Article 5 as of 2026‑10‑10. [11]

Jordan informed Nadia on Sep 8 that he was ill and would deliver Article 5 by Sep 12, but after Nadia’s follow‑up messages on Sep 16 and Sep 24 the freelancer did not respond, creating the impression of abandonment. [12][13][14]

Because one of the five articles (20 % of the total contract value) was not delivered, a proportional refund of $250 is warranted under the agreed pricing. [3]

Jordan will deliver the missing Article 5 within five business days; if Nadia declines the delivery, a $250 refund will be issued promptly. [15]

Given that four articles and the email sequence were fully delivered, approved, published, and used, the remainder of the chargeback is contested and should be reversed. [4][5][6][7][8][9]

Accordingly, PayPal should release $1,250 to the seller and approve the $250 partial refund to the buyer as the fair resolution. [2]
